Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Consider the following system of equations:
[MATH: {5x + 2y = − 1; − 4x − 3y = − 2]
Suppose we want to eliminate the variable [MATH: x] from the system using the elimination method.

Content:
First, notice that the coefficient of [MATH: x] in the first equation is [MATH: {\color{red}{5}},] while in the second equation it is [MATH: -{\color{blue}{4}}.]

Content:
So, if we multiply the first equation by [MATH: {\color{blue}{4}}] and the second equation by [MATH: {\color{red}{5}},] then the [MATH: x]-coefficient in the first and second equations respectively will become [MATH: 20] and [MATH: -20,] and these will cancel when we add the equations.

Content:
[MATH: {(5x + 2y = − 1) × (4); (− 4x − 3y = − 2) × (5)]

Content:
Now, when we add the two equations, the variable [MATH: x] will be eliminated:

Content:
[MATH: 20x + 8y|= − 4; − 20x − 15y|= − 10; (8y − 15y)|= (− 4 − 10); − 7y|= − 14; y|= 2]

Content:
Therefore, we have successfully eliminated the variable [MATH: x] from the system.

Now, when we add the two equations, the variable [MATH: a] will be eliminated:

[MATH: 12a + 8b|= − 8; − 12a + 9b|= − 9; (8b + 9b)|= (− 8 − 9); 17b|= − 17]

Therefore, the correct answer is the following:

Item 8 — Example: Solving a System of Equations by Eliminating the First Variable

Example Prompt:

EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Notice that the [MATH: x]-coefficient in the first equation is [MATH: {\color{red}2},] while in the second equation it is [MATH: -{\color{blue}3}.]

If we multiply the first equation by [MATH: {\color{blue}3}] and the second equation by [MATH: {\color{red}2},] then the [MATH: x]-coefficient in the first and second equations will become [MATH: 6] and [MATH: -6,] and these will cancel when we add the equations.

[MATH: {(2x − 3y = − 7) × (3); (− 3x + 4y = 8) × (2)]

Now, when we add the two equations, the variable [MATH: x] will be eliminated:

[MATH: 6x − 9y|= − 21; − 6x + 8y|= 16; (8y − 9y)|= (16 − 21); − y|= − 5; y|= 5]

So, the solution must have [MATH: y=5.] However, we still need to find [MATH: x.] To do this, we substitute [MATH: y=5] back into one of the equations. Let's choose the first equation:

[MATH: 2x − 3y|= − 7; 2x − 3(5)|= − 7; 2x − 15|= − 7; 2x|= 8; x|= 4]

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is [MATH: x=4] and [MATH: y=5], which can be written as [MATH: (4,5).]

Item 11 — Example: Solving a System of Equations by Eliminating the Second Variable

Explanation:
Notice that the coefficient of [MATH: y] in the first equation is [MATH: {\color{red}3},] while in the second equation it is [MATH: {\color{blue}4}.]

If we multiply the first equation by [MATH: {\color{blue}4}] and the second equation by [MATH: -{\color{red}3},] then the [MATH: y]-coefficient in the first and second equations will become [MATH: -12] and [MATH: 12,] and these will cancel when we add the equations.

[MATH: {(4x + 3y = 3) × (4); (5x + 4y = 5) × (− 3)]

Now, when we add the two equations, the variable [MATH: y] will be eliminated:

[MATH: 16x + 12y|= 12; − 15x − 12y|= − 15; (16x − 15x)|= (12 − 15); x|= − 3]

So, the solution must have [MATH: x=-3.] However, we still need to find [MATH: y.] To do this, we substitute [MATH: x=-3] back into one of the equations. Let's choose the first equation:

[MATH: 4x + 3y|= 3; 4(− 3) + 3y|= 3; − 12 + 3y|= 3; 3y|= 15; y|= 5]

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is [MATH: x=-3] and [MATH: y=5,] which can be written as [MATH: (-3,5).]
